units.title: Name what you can observe
units.lesson: A macule is a flat colour change. A papule is a raised solid lesion; a plaque is a broader raised area. An erosion involves superficial epithelial loss, whereas an ulcer extends deeper. These words describe appearance rather than identify a cause. Record the site and distribution before proposing a diagnosis. Numeric size cut-offs vary between terminology systems; this chapter uses qualitative distinctions.
units.question: Which term describes a flat colour change?
units.explanation: A macule changes colour without elevation.
rationales: Flat colour change fits a macule.

units.title: Build a useful examination record
units.lesson: Separate the history from examination findings. History records symptoms, duration, changes, medical conditions and medicines. Examination records observable features such as site and appearance. A diagnostic opinion is an interpretation of this evidence. A record should make it possible to follow the reasoning and identify information still missing; a label alone is not a complete assessment.
units.question: Which entry is an observation rather than a diagnosis?
choices: A red area on the left buccal mucosa
units.explanation: The first entry describes a finding without assigning a cause.

units.title: Understand what an image adds
units.lesson: Dental radiography uses ionizing radiation. CBCT reconstructs three-dimensional information; conventional dental radiographs are two-dimensional projections. More dimensions do not automatically make an examination necessary. An imaging question, relevant alternatives and radiation exposure must be considered. An image contributes evidence alongside history and examination; this lesson does not prescribe imaging for an individual.
units.question: What distinguishes CBCT data from a conventional dental projection?
units.explanation: CBCT provides 3-D information but still involves X-rays.
rationales: This is the relevant dimensional distinction.

units.title: Know the purpose of a biopsy
units.lesson: A biopsy obtains cells or tissue for examination, usually by a pathologist. Histological evidence can help establish the nature of a lesion. A photograph or surface description is not the same as microscopic examination. The educational distinction is between describing an appearance and investigating tissue; no sampling technique or patient decision is taught here.
units.question: What is the defining purpose of a biopsy?
choices: Obtain cells or tissue for examination
Assign a cause from colour alone
units.explanation: Biopsy supplies material for cellular or tissue examination.
rationales: Colour alone is not tissue analysis.

units.title: Name what you can observe · apply

units.question: A fictional atlas shows a solid elevation with an intact surface. Which description is best?
units.explanation: A papule is a solid raised lesion; an erosion loses epithelium and a macule is flat.
rationales: Erosion describes surface loss, not elevation.
units.hint: Ask whether tissue is raised or missing.

units.title: Build a useful examination record · apply
units.lesson: Close the notes. Apply the concept to this new example, then compare your reasoning with the explanation.
units.question: An examination note records “likely inflammatory disease” but no site or appearance. What is the most useful addition?
choices: Record the lesion site and morphology
Treat the tentative cause as an observation
units.explanation: An interpretation should be supported by recorded observations.
rationales: Site and morphology supply missing observations.
A tentative cause remains an interpretation.

units.title: Understand what an image adds · apply
units.lesson: Close the notes. Apply the concept to this new example, then compare your reasoning with the explanation.
units.question: A viva answer proposes CBCT solely because it is three-dimensional. Which response best addresses the reasoning?
choices: Define the imaging question and weigh the added information and exposure
Assume CBCT uses no ionizing radiation
units.explanation: Additional information must justify the examination; dimensionality alone is insufficient.
rationales: More dimensions do not establish necessity.
units.hint: Does extra detail automatically justify exposure?

units.question: Which additional information can a biopsy report provide beyond a surface photograph?
choices: The patient’s symptom duration without a history
A complete imaging-based lesion map by itself
units.explanation: Biopsy material permits cellular or tissue examination.
rationales: History is still needed for symptom duration.
This is the added scale of evidence.
Biopsy is not an imaging examination.
